analysis.one_liner: Increases damages and criminal penalties for copyright and trademark violations and expands federal enforcement against counterfeiting.
analysis.headline: Passed the Senate by unanimous consent and the House 381-41, and was signed into law on October 13, 2008 as Public Law 110-403.
analysis.plain_summary: This law raises the civil damages companies can win in trademark counterfeiting cases, adds criminal penalties including prison terms of up to life when counterfeit goods cause death, and lets the government seize and destroy property connected to copyright and counterfeiting offenses. It creates a White House Intellectual Property Enforcement Coordinator to coordinate enforcement across agencies, and authorizes tens of millions of dollars a year for FBI agents, federal prosecutors, and grants to state and local police to pursue intellectual property cases. The stated aims include protecting jobs and innovation and keeping dangerous counterfeit goods out of the supply chain; the enforcement machinery it builds primarily protects the assets of copyright and trademark owners.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of copyrights and trademarks — movie studios, record labels, software companies, luxury brands, and other manufacturers — get higher damages (treble damages in counterfeiting cases and statutory damages doubled to $1,000–$200,000 per counterfeit mark), new felony designations, forfeiture and restitution, a dedicated White House coordinator, and more FBI agents, prosecutors, and state and local grant money directed at their cases. Consumers also get some protection from dangerous counterfeit goods such as fake medicines and auto parts, since trafficking that causes serious injury or death now carries prison terms up to 20 years or life.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Copyright and trademark owners and brand manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the statutory damages available in counterfeiting cases, from $500–$100,000 to $1,000–$200,000 per counterfeit mark, and doubles the cap to $2 million, and makes treble damages the default unless a court finds extenuating circumstances.

Adds criminal penalties for trafficking in counterfeit goods that knowingly or recklessly cause serious bodily injury (up to 20 years) or death (any term of years or life), addressing counterfeit products that genuinely endanger buyers.

Creates a Senate-confirmed Intellectual Property Enforcement Coordinator in the Executive Office of the President to chair an interagency committee and develop a joint strategic plan against counterfeiting and piracy.

Requires at least 10 additional FBI agents for intellectual property crimes, two prosecutors for each Computer Hacking and Intellectual Property unit, and authorizes about $55 million a year for fiscal 2009–2013 for FBI, DOJ, and state and local enforcement grants.

Requires forfeiture, destruction, and restitution for criminal copyright, counterfeiting, bootlegging, and economic espionage offenses, and makes exporting unauthorized copies of copyrighted works an infringement just like importing them.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new FBI agents, federal prosecutors, forensic tools, and state and local grants — authorizations totaling roughly $55 million per year for five years. Individuals and small businesses accused of infringement face doubled and trebled damages, forfeiture of any property used to commit or facilitate an offense, and new liability for exporting copyrighted goods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people accused of infringement

drawbacks.text: Forfeiture reaches not only infringing goods but 'any property used, or intended to be used, in any manner or part to commit or facilitate' the offense, plus property derived from proceeds — meaning a person's other assets can be seized and destroyed over an intellectual property offense.

The bill extends copyright infringement liability to exportation of unauthorized copies, and provides for records impoundment in civil cases, expanding the reach of enforcement actions over goods and documents.

The federal enforcement money is directed at protecting private intellectual property — an area where the industries themselves already sue infringers — rather than at crimes with broader public benefit, and the grants require states to have specified anti-counterfeiting laws to qualify.

A fair objection supporters would raise: counterfeit goods are not a victimless matter — fake pharmaceuticals, auto parts, and consumer products can injure or kill buyers, and counterfeiting revenue is linked to organized crime, which the law's criminal penalties and FBI resources directly address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The provisions targeting counterfeit goods that cause injury or death, and the push to coordinate scattered federal enforcement efforts, have real public value. But the core of the law is a penalty-and-resources package for copyright and trademark owners: higher damages, asset forfeiture, and tens of millions in annual public spending aimed at protecting private business assets. The heaviest costs fall on taxpayers and on defendants facing harsher remedies, and the bill does little to address how aggressive intellectual property enforcement affects ordinary consumers of media and software.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent and the House passed it 381-41 under a fast-track procedure that skips amendments, and President Bush signed it on October 13, 2008.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Leahy on July 24, 2008 with 21 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, the bill was reported favorably by the Senate Judiciary Committee and placed on the Senate calendar in mid-September.

The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent on September 26, 2008, after the Judiciary Committee's amendments were withdrawn by unanimous consent; the version introduced in the Senate had authorized the Attorney General to bring civil copyright enforcement actions, a provision that does not appear in the enacted law.

The House took it up under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure allowing no amendments and requiring a two-thirds vote — and passed it 381-41 on September 28, 2008, with Democrats voting 205-22 and Republicans 176-19.
It was signed by the President on October 13, 2008 and became Public Law 110-403.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copyright and trademark industries gained a White House enforcement coordinator, more FBI agents and prosecutors, higher damages, and new forfeiture tools. The dropped provision that would have had the Justice Department sue infringers on copyright owners' behalf means even the critics came out partly better than the original bill would have had it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was strongly bipartisan: it cleared the Senate by unanimous consent and passed the House 381-41, with 205 of 234 Democrats and 176 of 199 Republicans voting yes.

industries.industry: Entertainment and software copyright holders (studios, record labels, software publishers)
industries.note: The law adds felony designations, forfeiture and restitution for criminal copyright offenses, makes exporting unauthorized copies an infringement, and adds FBI agents and grant money aimed at their cases. Stronger enforcement raises the stakes for individuals accused of sharing or selling copyrighted works, a cost borne largely by consumers and small sellers.

industries.industry: Trademark-owning brands (luxury goods, apparel, consumer products)
industries.note: Trademark owners get default treble damages and statutory damages doubled to $1,000–$200,000 per counterfeit mark, up to $2 million, plus forfeiture and export prohibitions. On dangerous counterfeits their interest runs with the public's, since fake medicines and parts genuinely harm buyers.

New criminal penalties of up to 20 years or life for counterfeit trafficking that causes serious injury or death, and a joint strategic plan aimed at keeping counterfeit goods out of the supply chain, serve both brand owners and consumer safety.

The law authorizes $25 million a year in grants for police training, overtime, and equipment to pursue intellectual property cases, a new revenue stream for local agencies — though the funds are earmarked for protecting private rights holders.
